en: Preface to the *Zhao Lun* by Huida, composed in his own ignorance as a preface to the four treatises—*Zongben*, *Buxian*, etc.—written by the Dharma Master Shi Sengzhao of Chang’an:

There is one of beautiful virtue who transcends speech while simultaneously abiding in silence; in establishing the fundamental source, every sentence deeply penetrates the Buddha-mind. It clarifies...

In conclusion, I declare that every word is fully attuned to the various teachings. It is my humble good fortune to have encountered this sublime sound; whenever I open and examine it, I cannot help but dance with joy.
I vow that throughout all future lives, I shall devote my entire life to its propagation and exposition. Now, the Way of the Spirits is formless, and the subtlety of the mind is difficult to depict;

I have merely composed this brief preface, leaving it to future sages to judge. For as for the profound meaning of the Great Division, its very name is "Original Non-existence" (Benwu); thus, [it remains beyond words].
The purpose of these expositions is to point toward the reality-mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and open the path of the Dharma of emptiness; nothing surpasses the True and the Conventional for this end.

Therefore, the Two Truths are explained next to reveal the gateway of the Buddha’s teachings. As for the cause that is perfectly correct, none is superior to Prajñā; as for the ultimate fruit, there is only Nirvāṇa.
Thus, at the conclusion, the "Twofold Mystery" is initiated to clarify the abode of all the Sages. Although the fundamental nature of emptiness is used to model the source, [it remains the ultimate].

There is no fundamental source that can be named; the discourse on the source transcends words and is not a realm where the mind operates. Thus, non-transmigration corresponds to the conventional, yet the conventional is unborn.
Non-reality serves as reality, though "reality" is but a verbal designation. If one can revere this single path of the two truths beyond speech, [one attains liberation].
Thus, the merit of tranquil illumination is manifest; therefore, while Prajñā is without cognition, the virtue of the Nameless arises, and Nirvāṇa is beyond designation.

I maintain that this teaching is complete and perfect, exhausting the profound ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom. It is vast and boundless, reaching the ultimate limits of the essence and characteristics of all phenomena.
The First Volume of the *Honglun*. This is the work of Master Sengzhao.
A Brief Commentary on the *Zhao Lun*, Volume One, composed by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Deqing of Mount Kuang.
*Zhao lun*:
"Zhao" is the name of the author, namely Sengzhao; he was commonly referred to as Master Zhao at that time. "Lun" refers to the treatise established by him;
thus, the title uses the person's name to designate the work. The Master was a preeminent disciple of Kumārajīva and participated in the translation bureau to translate various scriptures.

Having attended Master Kumārajīva for a long time, he attained a profound understanding of the true nature of reality (*tathatā*). At that time, as the Buddha-dharma had only recently arrived from the West, its great principles had not yet been fully elucidated.
The people of the age mostly favored the discourses on emptiness found in the works of Laozi and Zhuangzi;

even the śramaṇas and sons of the Śākya followed this trend, frequently using the doctrine of emptiness to explain Buddhist meanings and each establishing it as their own school. For instance, Daoheng of the Jin dynasty expounded upon "Non-being" (*wu*).

Regarding the *Xinlun* (Treatise on the Mind) composed by Daolin of the Eastern Jin, the *Jisèyouxuānlùn* (Treatise on Wandering the Profound through the Suchness of Form), and the *Benwúlùn* (Treatise on Non-existence at the Root) composed by Zhu Fatai of the Jin—all these fall into the trap of speaking of "non-existence" based on appearances, thereby falling entirely into the view of nihilism.

Because the Master [Sengzhao] lamented that the Great Way was not yet clearly understood, he composed these four treatises to shatter false attachments; this is the fundamental intent of his discourse. As for the term "discourse" (*lùn*), it refers to the hypothetical establishment of a respondent...

Preface: Examining and analyzing through logical inference to reveal correct principles and demolish false attachments; because it treats both person and phenomena as dual reflections, it is called the *Zhao Lun*.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Sengzhao of Chang’an during the Later Qin dynasty.
Fu Jian possessed the state, occupying Guanzhong and styling himself the Great Qin. When Yao Chang usurped the throne and established his own rule, he was likewise styled Qin;
therefore, the histories distinguish between the two periods. Upon the death of Yao Chang, his son Yao Xing succeeded to the kingdom, during which time Master Shi translated the scriptures.
At the time of his rise, the Duke [Fu Jian] styled himself the Later Qin. According to the biography of the Duke, it states briefly: "The Dharma Master Sengzhao was a native of Jingzhao.
In his youth, his family was poor, and he worked as a hired scribe. Consequently, he read widely through the *Zi* and *Shi* classics;

his aspirations were inclined toward the profound and the mysterious (*xuan*), and he constantly took the teachings of Laozi and Zhuangzi as the essentials of his heart. Thereupon, he sighed and said: 'Beautiful indeed they are! Yet, as for their resting the spirit in the dark mystery...'"

The methods he had accumulated were still not entirely perfected. Later, upon seeing the old *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, he received it with joy and veneration, saying, "Only now do I know where I truly belong.
Because of this, he left the household life; at the age of twenty, he became a śramaṇa, and his fame resounded throughout the Three Commanderies.

When Master Kumārajīva was in Guzang, Sengzhao fled there to seek his protection. Upon conversing with him, Kumārajīva was struck with amazement and remarked, "He is a dragon or an elephant among those of the Dharma.
When they returned to Guanzhong, Sengzhao meticulously edited and determined the meaning of the sūtras and śāstras. Scholars from all quarters flocked to him like the spokes of a wheel;

though they launched difficult challenges and attacked him from every side, Sengzhao met each point as it arose and resolved them, all exceeding their expectations. He composed the *Prajñā-aprativijñapti-śāstra* (Treatise on the Non-cognition of Prajñā), which Kumārajīva read.
He said, "I understand; I shall not thank you. I shall merely bow to you as a fellow scholar. He transmitted this discourse to Mount Kuang.
Liu Yimin, considering it similar to the works of Master Yuan (Huiyuan), clapped his thighs and sighed, saying, "Never before has such a thing been seen!

He further composed treatises such as "The Non-transmigration of Things," all of which exhaustively capture the subtle and the profound. The Ruler of Qin held his writings in especially high esteem, and they were circulated both within and beyond the borders. [His] age...
He passed away at the age of thirty-two; those of his time lamented his early demise.

Regarding "The Fundamental Basis of the Tenets" (*Jōhon-gishū*): this indicates that there is a fundamental basis for the tenets upon which his arguments are established. This is because the four treatises were not composed at a single time.

Once the treatise was completed, he then unified it with the fundamental tenet as its governing principle. This fundamental tenet is rooted in the one mind, which serves to exhaustively investigate the source of all phenomena—delusion and enlightenment, the ordinary and the sage.
Just as the *Awakening of Faith* takes the one mind as its tenet, possessing both its phenomena (*dharma*) and its meaning (*artha*), it is therefore called the "Fundamental Tenet and Meaning."
"Original Non-existence," "Ultimate Reality," "Dharma-nature," "Essential Emptiness," and "The Convergence of Conditions" are but one single meaning.
This establishes the fundamental tenets and distinguishes the teachings, serving as the basis for the four treatises. As for "Original Non-existence":

it points directly to the quiescent single mind, wherein not a single dharma exists; it is free from all marks and utterly transcends both the holy and the ordinary. Therefore, it is called "Original Non-existence. It is not... [text ends]
One deduces that they are non-existent because all dharmas are manifestations produced by the single mind following conditions.

The mind is fundamentally unarisen; it arises only through the convergence of conditions. Therefore, it is called "the convergence of conditions. Since all dharmas arise from conditions, they lack any inherent substance.

Because they arise from conditions, they are empty; therefore, it is called "emptiness of nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). Because they are transformations of the entirety of True Suchness (*tathatā*), [they are thus empty].

It is called the *dharmatā*. All phenomena (*dharma*) are constituted by the *dharmatā* of true thusness (*tathatā*). Since true thusness is without marks (*animitta*), the fundamental substance of all phenomena is quiescent;

therefore, it is called the "true aspect" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Thus, original non-existence constitutes the substance of the one mind, while the convergence of conditions constitutes the function of the one mind.
True aspect, *dharmatā*, and the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) are all meanings of the myriad phenomena produced by the one mind.
Therefore, it is said that there is but a single principle. Based on the dharma of the one mind, these four treatises are established:

"Non-transmigration" corresponds to the conventional truth, and "Non-true" corresponds to the ultimate truth. The two truths constitute the objects of contemplation; Prajñā is the mind that contemplates them;
the three treatises are the cause, and Nirvāṇa is the fruit. Thus, the first [treatise] constitutes the essential substance of the school.
Why is this so? (This section raises four arguments, each with its own underlying tenet. All phenomena arise through the convergence of conditions;
this [passage] below marks and clarifies the essential substance of the tenet of non-transmigration. Within the quiescent single mind, phenomena fundamentally do not exist.
Being originally non-existent yet now existing, it is said that they "arise through the convergence of conditions."
Arising occurs through the convergence of conditions; thus, that which has not yet arisen does not exist. When conditions disperse, it ceases.
This reveals that the mind is fundamentally unarisen and arises only through conditions; it is not that the mind itself gives birth [to itself]. For arising is fundamentally non-arising.
Therefore, cessation also has cessation as its condition; it is not the cessation of the mind. Thus, the meaning of the single mind that is neither born nor ceasing is made manifest.
If it were truly existent, then being existent, there would be no cessation.
This serves as a counter-argument to demonstrate that all dependently arisen phenomena (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*) are not substantially real (*dravyasat*). "Real" means truly existent.

If the fruits of phenomena were substantially real, they ought not to disperse and perish according to conditions. Since they now perish in accordance with conditions, phenomena are not substantially real.

Inferring from this, we know that although things presently exist, their nature is eternally empty of itself. Because their nature is eternally empty of itself, it is called "emptiness of nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
By observing all phenomena through the principle of dependent origination and dependent cessation, one knows that although they appear to exist now, they do not exist in reality.

Because their essence is eternally and inherently empty, they are described as being "empty of intrinsic nature" (svabhāva-śūnya). Because their essence is eternally and inherently empty, they are described as being "empty of intrinsic nature."
Because its nature is empty, it is called "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*).

The true nature of all phenomena is precisely *tathatā* (suchness). The nature of *tathatā* is empty. Because the nature of *tathatā* manifests and constitutes all phenomena, every phenomenon is entirely true.
This is truly because the nature of *tathatā* is empty; therefore, the nature of all phenomena is empty. This is termed "Dharma."
Nature. Such is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); therefore, it is called the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
The nature of all phenomena is, in its entirety, True Suchness (tathatā). The mark of True Suchness is originally without marks. The nature of phenomena is thus.
It is thus: because it is quiescent and free from characteristics, it is called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The true mark is itself non-existent; it is not made non-existent through some external effort. Therefore, it is named "original non-existence" (*mūlābhāva*).
The true mark is the substantial reality of *tathatā*. Now, since it follows conditions to manifest as all phenomena (*dharmas*), every single phenomenon is...
Truly so. If one contemplates that all phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely true, then one realizes that there is not a single phenomenon that can be grasped by the mind.
This means that it is not necessary to employ inference to make them non-existent; rather, phenomena are fundamentally non-existent from the start.

Since the myriad phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, how could there be even a hair’s breadth of anything that can be moved or altered? Contemplating all phenomena through this lens, the principle of non-transmigration becomes vividly clear to the mind and eye.
This clarifies the fundamental tenet of non-transmigration.
To say that things are neither existent nor non-existent (this marks the fundamental tenet of Non-True Emptiness) means that they are not the "existence" of those with views of permanence,
nor the "non-existence" of those with heterodox views of annihilation.
This indicates the attachments to be refuted by the established doctrine. "Not so" (不如) means not comparable.
Ordinary people and non-Buddhists dogmatically cling to all phenomena as truly existent, while others stubbornly hold to them as being annihilated into non-existence;
these are precisely what is to be refuted. By using the word "not" (不) alone to refute them, it is said: "neither existent nor non-existent."
If one regards existence as existent, then one regards non-existence as nonexistent;
this is a conceptual construction. If one regards all phenomena as truly existent, one falls into the view of eternalism;
if one regards all phenomena as truly nonexistent, one falls into the view of nihilism.
Now, one who does not maintain [the notions of] non-existence while contemplating dharmas may be said to recognize the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of dharmas;
this demonstrates right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*). Under "maintaining non-existence" (*cun wu*), the character "existence" (*you*) should be added.

It means that by not maintaining the two views of existence and non-existence while contemplating dharmas, one may be said to recognize the true mark of dharmas. For the two views of existence and non-existence are inverted (*viparyāsa*).
It is seen. Although one contemplates existence, there is no grasping at signs. Thus, the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) are the characteristics of signlessness;
the mind of the sage dwells in non-dwelling.

This refers to the benefit derived from emerging from contemplation. It means that by observing all phenomena while remaining free from the two views of existence and non-existence, each phenomenon is found to be quiescent.

Thus, although phenomena exist, one does not grasp at their marks. When one does not grasp at the marks of phenomena, they are, in their very essence, suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore, marks are themselves the mark of the markless.

All marks being markless, their nature is quiescent emptiness. This is what is meant by... [the object of]... (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly with "斯則所". The translation reflects this truncation.)
The objects of contemplation are empty; when objects are empty, the mind is naturally quiescent. Therefore, the mind of the sage is a dwelling in non-dwelling.
This is the emptiness of the mind. When both mind and objects are empty, how could there be anything that is not quiescent?
The three vehicles equally contemplate the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) and thereby attain the Way. "Emptiness of nature" refers to the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
Because one perceives the true reality of phenomena, it is called "right contemplation. Were it otherwise, it would constitute "erroneous contemplation.
If those of the two vehicles do not perceive this principle, they are inverted.

This explains the person who is capable of contemplation by means of the Dharma. Those of the three vehicles equally contemplate the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) and thereby attain the fruits of the Path.
However, this emptiness of the nature of all phenomena is itself the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). One who is able to perceive the true mark of all phenomena [is the one so described].
This alone constitutes right contemplation. Even if those of the Two Vehicles do not perceive this principle, they would be as deluded and inverted as ordinary worldlings.

This is because all phenomena are, in their entirety, the true mark (*dharmatā*). What the Two Vehicles perceive is a partial emptiness, yet this too is the true mark of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
If it were not the true mark of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, how could they realize the fruits of the Path? The intent is that the Dharma is one.
The persons are different; therefore, it is difficult to clarify below.
For this reason, there is no difference in the way the three vehicles contemplate the Dharma; the distinction lies only in the magnitude of their minds.
This clarifies that while the Dharma is one, the persons are different. [The opponent] submits an objection, saying: "If the three vehicles equally perceive the one Dharma, why..."
Regarding the fact that there are differences in the fruits of realization, the answer is: In reality, the methods of contemplation for the Three Vehicles are no different;

it is only because the mind has degrees of magnitude that the fruits realized differ. This is sufficient to know that the Dharma is fundamentally one, yet because the minds of people differ in their magnitude, the fruits realized are not the same.
This is due to grasping at or not grasping at signs; it is not that the Dharma itself is different.
It is just like three animals crossing a river. The river is originally one, yet because the three animals differ in size, the depth they traverse is not uniform.
This is because while there are three animals, the river is not three. To examine the intent behind establishing this argument:

it is likely that "non-transmigration" corresponds to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and "non-reality" corresponds to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). These two truths constitute the objects of contemplation. The *prajñā*...
If taken as the wisdom capable of contemplation, then object and wisdom are the cause and nirvana is the fruit;
since the three vehicles are those who are able to cultivate this, there is indeed a profound reason for its inclusion among the fundamental tenets of our school.
"Upāya-prajñā" is a designation for "Great Wisdom.
This indicates that the fundamental principle of Prajñā is non-cognition. In Sanskrit it is called *upāya*, which here means "expedient means"; *prajñā*... [is wisdom].

This is called "wisdom" (prajñā). Because it possesses the wisdom of skillful means (upāya), it is termed "Great Wisdom" (mahā-prajñā). If it lacks skillful means, it is merely called "solitary wisdom.
Therefore, that which grasps only biased emptiness is not Great Wisdom. The preceding two [sections] discussed the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional.
That which is the object of contemplation is now the *upāya-prajñā* (expedient wisdom), while that which is the contemplating mind is the *prajñā* (wisdom).
Together they illuminate the two truths, neither grasping at existence nor non-existence, and thus do not fall into the two extremes; hence it is called "Great Wisdom" (*mahā-prajñā*).
The true reality of all phenomena is called *prajñā*. To be able to realize it without manifesting [it as a fixed form] is the merit of *upāya*.
To adaptively transform sentient beings is called *upāya*. To remain unstained by worldly entanglements is the power of *prajñā*.
This explains the meaning of "Great Wisdom" (Mahāprajñā). To be able to perceive the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is what is called *prajñā*.
Although one contemplates emptiness, one does not realize [nirvana] prematurely; rather, one continues to engage in the work of delivering sentient beings through skillful means (*upāya*).

This is due to the efficacy of *upāya*. Adapting to and transforming sentient beings is the function of skillful means. Thus, although one enters the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one is not defiled by worldly afflictions (*kleśa*).
This all relies entirely upon the power of *prajñā*. Therefore, when a Bodhisattva contemplates emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the myriad practices (*saṃskāra*) boil forth;
yet when they engage with existence (*bhava*), the single Way remains pure. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Wisdom without skillful means (*upāya*) is bondage;

wisdom with skillful means is liberation. Skillful means without wisdom is bondage; skillful means with wisdom is liberation. Thus, they simultaneously illuminate both truths (*satyadvaya*), neither grasping at existence nor non-existence.
Because of these characteristics, one is able to emerge from emptiness and enter into the provisional without obstruction; hence it is called "Great Wisdom" (Mahāprajñā).
Thus, while the gate of *prajñā* contemplates emptiness, the gate of *upāya* engages with existence. Yet, in engaging with existence, one never begins by losing sight of the void.
Therefore, one constantly dwells within existence without being defiled by it; one does not loathe existence while contemplating emptiness. Thus, one contemplates emptiness without realizing it.

This is what is called the power of a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇabala*). Expedient means and wisdom are fully present. The power of a single thought-moment—expedient means and wisdom are fully present.
Reflect well; this is clearly intelligible.
This further clarifies the meaning of non-realization and non-defilement. Because *prajñā* (wisdom) illuminates only emptiness, while *upāya* (skillful means) engages only with existence;
because one engages with existence without losing sight of the void, this relies on the power of *prajñā*, and thus one dwells in existence without being defiled.
Because one contemplates emptiness without loathing existence, one contemplates emptiness without taking realization as a goal; this relies on *upāya*.
This is the merit of harmony. It is thus the two truths of emptiness and existence, which are not different; it is the one mind in which the provisional and the real are non-dual.

These are simultaneously and dualistically illumined, such that existence and cessation are unimpeded. Therefore, it is said that within the power of a single thought-moment, both skillful means and wisdom are fully present.
If you can clearly understand through careful reflection, exert yourself in focused contemplation so that it becomes distinct;
then the mind and its objects will become vividly clear, provisional and ultimate truths will manifest together, and you shall effortlessly achieve wondrous resonance with the truth.
Regarding the Truth of the Extinction of Nirvāṇa: it is simply the exhaustion of the fetters. Thus, birth and death are eternally extinguished; for this reason, it is called "extinction.
There is no separate place of extinction apart from this.
This indicates that Nirvana is fundamentally without name. What is called *niyuan* (Nirvana) is also termed *niepan*.

That which is designated as the Truth of Cessation (*kṣayadharma*) is simply the exhaustion of the fetters of affliction. Specifically, it refers to the thorough exhaustion of the five abodes; thus, the two types of death are forever extinguished.
This is the eternal extinction of birth and death, which is what is meant by "cessation. It is not that there exists some separate place of cessation apart from this.

Returning [to the source], there is likewise no real name by which it can be designated; therefore, it is said that Nirvāṇa is nameless. This is the fundamental principle of the Four Treatises (*Catuḥśāstra*).

Taking the One Mind as the basis, one speaks of the Two Truths of neither existence nor non-existence. Through the contemplation that is neither knowing nor not-knowing, one realizes the One Mind that is neither born nor extinguished.
Cause and effect merge in profound darkness, wondrously harmonizing within the center of the circle. This is the core tenet.
The meaning of the fundamental principle is exhausted in this.
"On the Non-Transmigration of Things," Chapter One:

This treatise establishes that conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); it serves as the object of contemplation. "Things" (*vastu*) refers to the myriad phenomena that constitute the objects of contemplation.
"Dharma does not transmigrate" refers to the true mark (*dharmatā*) of the very essence of all phenomena. Through the deluded perceptions of ordinary people, phenomena appear as if subject to flux;

yet when viewed through *prajñā*, one suddenly perceives the true mark of all phenomena as being, in their very essence, quiescent, eternally constant, and utterly devoid of any characteristic of movement or change—what is called "not a single dharma that can be shifted or turned."
Because that which arises through conditions is empty of intrinsic nature, each and every phenomenon is, in its very essence, fundamentally non-transmigratory.

It is not that the characteristics transmigrate while the nature remains non-transmigratory; rather, it is because one can perceive that every single thing is non-transmigratory that things themselves are the truth.

When there is truth, not a single dharma exists that can be grasped by the mind. Observing the conventional from this perspective, the conventional is itself the truth. This is truly because the principle is fully realized.

All things are accomplished; every phenomenon is true. Thus, the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all dharmas is revealed. The Master of the Treatise takes the *Vimalakīrti* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as his primary authorities and deeply awakens to the true mark.
He regards the non-transmigration [of phenomena] as the conventional, and realizes that within the conventional there is the true.
The principle of non-transmigration becomes manifest before his mind’s eye.

Now, the passing away of birth and death and the alternating shifts of cold and heat are the natural conditions of all things in flux; this is the common understanding of people. I, however, maintain that it is not so.

To clarify the principle of non-transmigration, one must first establish the characteristics of transmigration as the object of contemplation; the essential point lies in [realizing] non-transmigration within that very transmigration.

This is because one perceives non-transmigration; it is not that phenomena transmigrate while their nature does not, but rather that people, being deluded, claim there is transmigration, whereas when people awaken, there is no transmigration.
Thus, it is said that this is the common sentiment of humanity, yet I maintain that this is not so.

The Master [Sengzhao] has attained a wondrous realization of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), and therefore he refutes these views in general. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Not as the three realms perceive the three realms."
Where it is scorched by great fires, this land is peaceful and secure. It is like the waters of the Ganges: what humans see as water, ghosts see as fire.
The distinction between delusion and awakening is likewise based on this.
What is this? (This explains the causes of delusion and awakening. The *Prabhāsa-sūtra* states: "Phenomena have neither going nor coming; they are without movement or transition.
This citation establishes the definitive essence of the school's tenet. Regarding this meaning, the seventh fascicle of that same sutra says:
"All phenomena are immovable; therefore, all phenomena neither go nor come," and so forth. This is precisely what the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* refers to when it says: "This dharma abides..."
"The dharma-position: the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding. This refers to the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;

in their very essence, they are *tathatā* (suchness), fundamentally devoid of the characteristics of coming, going, movement, or change. When viewed with the Buddha-eye, they are empty, quiescent, and profound stillness; it is only through the deluded vision of ordinary beings that there appears to be flux.
The essential purport of the "Treatise on Non-Flux" takes this as its primary tenet.
Now, as for the activity of the immovable: how could one seek stillness by abandoning movement? One must necessarily seek stillness within all movements;

this is the definition of the essence derived from the fundamental principle (*zong*). To investigate the purport of the immovable is, in fact, to perceive the true permanence through the very objects of movement;
it is not to abandon movement in order to seek stillness. This is because all phenomena are entirely constituted by principle (*li*); every dharma is thus.

True. It is the essence itself that is eternally abiding; one does not seek principle apart from phenomena. Therefore, it speaks only of the non-transiency of phenomena, not of the non-transiency of principle.
Because one perceives non-transiency through the very nature of things, it says: "One must seek stillness within all movement. The arguments established in this treatise consist of four sections.
The first explains that the objective realm is non-transient by means of movement and stillness. Next, regarding...
The first [section] uses the objective realm to clarify that things do not transmigrate. The third uses the ancient and the present to clarify that time does not transmigrate.
The fourth uses time to clarify that cause and effect do not transmigrate; this is the first of those.

One must seek stillness within all movement; therefore, although there is movement, one is always still. One does not abandon movement to seek stillness; therefore, although there is stillness, one does not depart from movement.

This is the explanation of the meaning based on the essence. When one necessarily seeks stillness within movement, even though ten thousand movements are arrayed before one, the mind and its objects remain profoundly tranquil.
Therefore, it is said that although there is movement, one is always still. If one does not abandon movement to seek stillness, then the single Way remains empty and spacious;
though responding to conditions in a complex interplay, it never loses its essential meeting point. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"Without leaving the site of enlightenment, one pervades all places. This is what is meant by: "The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm, universally appearing before all sentient beings."

Responding to conditions and meeting with sentient beings, there is nowhere he does not reach; yet he constantly remains upon this seat of Bodhi. Without awakening to this principle, it is difficult to clarify the essential teaching that movement and stillness are non-dual.
Thus, movement and stillness have never been different from the outset, yet those who are deluded perceive them as distinct.

Consequently, true words are obstructed by contentious debate, and the path of the fundamental doctrine is stifled by a fondness for novelty. Therefore, the ultimate states of tranquility and agitation are not easily described.
This is an analysis of delusion based on the meaning [of the teachings]. In reality, motion and stillness share a single source; they are fundamentally non-dual and have never been different.
It is only that those who are deluded perceive them falsely as distinct and each cling to one extreme.

Thus, regarding the true words—such as the definitive teachings cited above concerning "not coming or going" and "neither moving nor shifting"—because of these divergent views, the words of ultimate truth... [are obscured].

Stuck in competitive debate, they fail to achieve understanding. Consequently, the true doctrine of the One Vehicle cannot be fully elucidated, as it is instead suppressed by arguments that favor novelty—such as claims that "the mind has no root" or "is fundamentally vast and empty.

These views all fail to comprehend the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) and give rise to false heterodoxies. For this reason, the ultimate point regarding the extremes of stillness and agitation is difficult to fathom.

**Discourse on Non-True Emptiness, Part Two** This discourse treats "emptiness that is not empty" (*bù zhēn kōng*) as the realm of the True Truth (*satyadharma*) to be contemplated. There are two aspects to this non-trueness.

There is existence. This emptiness is not a void of annihilation, but is wondrous emptiness (*prajñā-śūnyatā*). This state of being neither existent nor empty constitutes the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
