with a vacant mind and profound discernment, there is nothing hidden that it does not illuminate.

Therefore, when responding externally to the manifold movements of phenomena, it forgets knowledge and extinguishes illumination, closing off wisdom and silencing the ear—possessing no claim to knowledge. Yet internally, it merges with the Principle, where true knowledge shines alone. Thus...
It is said that the Pratyekabuddha dwells in profound stillness; this is what is meant by "having no knowledge, yet knowing nothing that is not known.

Thus, while wisdom possesses the mirror-like discernment that penetrates the most profound mysteries, it is itself "without knowledge" (realizing true wisdom through internal realization). Spirit, for its part, possesses the function of responding to and harmonizing with circumstances.
Yet there is no deliberation [in this]. (Wisdom and skill respond outwardly. Because the spirit has no deliberation, it can alone reign beyond the world;
because wisdom has no knowing, it can profoundly illuminate that which lies outside of affairs.
This analytical contemplation serves to manifest the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real. Real wisdom illuminates the principle;

therefore, it possesses a discernment that penetrates the profound depths. Its illuminating essence stands alone, such that both mind and object are forgotten, and thus there is no [discursive] knowing. "Spirit" refers to provisional wisdom.
Bowing in compliance with the various capacities of sentient beings, there is thus the function of responsive engagement. Responding without thought, there is no deliberation.
Because one responds without thought, things cannot cause affliction; thus, one alone reigns beyond the world. When wisdom is without knowing, the object and the mind meet;
as reality is encountered in every event, one is able to illuminate that which lies beyond events. Therefore, one does not abide in non-action.

Not abandoning the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), they manifest both the provisional and the ultimate simultaneously; observing all with equal vision and illuminating all at once—this is the mind of the Sage.
Although wisdom transcends worldly affairs, it has never been devoid of them; although the spirit stands beyond the world, it remains within the realm throughout the day.

Thus, by bowing and looking up, he accords with transformation, responding without end. There is nothing obscure that he does not perceive, yet there is no trace of the act of illumination. This, then, is the sphere of non-knowing.
This is known as the convergence of the sagely spirit (*shen*).
This explains why the two types of wisdom operate simultaneously: because reality is encountered in every phenomenon, although wisdom transcends phenomena, it has never been devoid of them;
because the spirit, though beyond the mundane world, does not abandon the salvation of sentient beings, therefore throughout the day...
Within this realm, because the two types of wisdom observe in unison, the Sage looks downward and upward, conforming to the transformations of the world.
Thus, his provisional wisdom responds to beings without end yet remains untainted; his ultimate wisdom perceives nothing hidden yet possesses no merit of illumination.
This is why it is called the "knowledge of the non-knowing" of sage-wisdom; it is where the divine mind of sage-wisdom reaches profound union.
Observing the Sage’s mind through this, the purport of Prajñā becomes manifest.
Yet, as for its substance (its essence), it is substantial yet not existent; it is empty yet not non-existent; it exists yet cannot be discussed.
"Is it not only through sage-like wisdom?
This clarifies that the essence of prajñā transcends both existence and non-existence. Prajñā possesses an inherently real essence;
yet, being without marks, it cannot be seen. Therefore, it is said to be 'real yet not existent. It is empty, numinous, profoundly still, and yet its illumination and function [are ever-present]."
It is always thus; therefore, it is said to be empty yet not non-existent. Regarding that which exists but cannot be discussed, the meaning is derived from the *Zhuangzi*:
"Beyond the six realms, the sage preserves [the mystery] without discussing it. This clarifies that Prajñā is not an object within the sphere of ordinary cognition or views;
therefore, one should simply preserve it without discussion, as it cannot be reached by words.
What is it? (It is subtle. If one wishes to say it exists, it has no form and no name; if one wishes to say it does not exist, the sages rely upon it for their spiritual power.
This clarifies that *prajñā* belongs neither to existence nor non-existence. If one wishes to say it exists, it lacks any characteristics and cannot be defined by name or appearance;
yet if one wishes to say it does not exist, the sages possess profound insight into the myriad operations of the world, and their responsive applications are never deficient.
Therefore, it cannot be named by means of existence or non-existence.
The Sage attains spiritual power through this; thus, while being empty, he does not lose his illumination. Being without form and without name, his illumination does not lose its emptiness.

The following clarifies that Prajñā is a single source of both quiescence and illumination; its essence and function are simultaneously manifested, and its provisional and ultimate aspects are concurrently revealed.

When emptiness does not lose its illumination, it is quiescent yet ever-illuminating; thus, the essence is not separate from the function. When illumination does not lose its emptiness, it is illuminating yet ever-quiescent;
thus, the function is not separate from the essence.
Because illumination does not lose its emptiness, it remains blended and unchanging. Because emptiness does not lose its illumination, it moves in order to engage with the coarse.

This precisely clarifies that the provisional and the real are manifested together. Because illumination does not lose its emptiness, the wisdom of skillful means responds externally to the world, blending and harmonizing all things, yet its essence remains limpid and immutable—*yu* meaning change. Because emptiness does not lose its illumination...

Therefore, while true wisdom is internally realized, it does not abandon the salvation of sentient beings. "Coarse" refers to manifesting within the three realms and responding according to their various types.
Thus, as the illumination becomes ever more profound, its application becomes ever more extensive.
Therefore, the application of sagely wisdom has never been suspended for even a moment; yet when sought within formal appearances, it cannot be found for even a moment.
This establishes the principle that quiescence and illumination are simultaneous.

Because the provisional and the real are non-dual, the Sage encompasses all phenomena and moves through the four modes of birth, never for a single thought-moment abandoning the realm of sentient beings. In truth, he seeks [nothing].
The traces of the functioning of that wisdom cannot be apprehended.
Thus, Ratnakūṭa says: "One manifests through the absence of mind and thought. The *Ratnāloka-sūtra* states:
"Without moving from equal enlightenment, one establishes all dharmas. Therefore, although the traces of the sages are manifold, their ultimate aim is but one.

This citation from two sutras establishes the principle that stillness and illumination share a single source. If a sage were to act with a deliberate mind, they would possess form and characteristics that could be apprehended;
however, because they manifest through the absence of mental intention, their physical appearance is like the moon reflected in water and their preaching of the Dharma is like an echo in a valley.
Although they can be seen and heard, in reality, if one seeks them, they cannot be found.
It is attained. Because all phenomena are established through the unmoving perfect enlightenment, the Dharma-realm pervades everywhere without departing from its own place.
Thus, although the traces of the sages are manifold, they are all the pervasive distribution of the Dharmakāya; therefore, it is said that their ultimate aim is one and the same.

Therefore, through *prajñā*, one may illuminate while remaining empty; the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) may be known while being extinguished; the myriad movements may be quiescent while being engaged;
and the sage’s response may be enacted while being non-existent. This is to know while not knowing, and to act while not acting.
What more is there to know? What more is there to do?
This summarizes that in *prajñā*, stillness and illumination are non-dual, and existence and extinction mutually integrate.

Since the preceding discussion has shown that the Sage’s mind thus manifests both essence and function simultaneously, although the essence of *prajñā* is ultimately void, one can, through that very voidness, exercise its illuminating function.
"Extinction" (*wang*) means cessation. Although the realm of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) transcends all marks, it can be known by means of that very transcendence of marks.
Although the myriad movements are chaotic, one can find stillness within movement. Although the Sage’s response is non-action (*wuwei*), one can act through that very non-action.
Thus, the sagely wisdom does not know yet knows itself; it does not act yet acts of itself. By following this...

Existence and extinction are mutually integrated; thus, essence and function are non-dual. The preceding section reveals their simultaneous existence, while the following section reveals their simultaneous extinction.
How could one know them? What could one do? In reality, there is neither knowing nor acting. The main treatise above is concluded.
Below follows the questions and answers that resolve doubts, consisting of eighteen sections.

The objection states: (First is the "Knowing Without Arrogance" objection. It follows from what was said previously: "Wisdom has the power to penetrate the profound, yet there is no [conscious] knowing; the spirit has the function of responding to circumstances, yet there is no deliberation. Thus, these two phrases are cited to raise the objection. The intent is to say:

since there is both knowing and responding, how can one claim there is no knowing and no responding? It is simply that the Sage possesses knowing yet does not boast of it. Now, the true mind of the Sage is uniquely luminous.

Each and every thing is illuminated; responding and receiving [them] is without fixed method. Movement accords with the event; each and every thing is illuminated. Thus one knows there is nothing left behind.

(The myriad realms are viewed as equal. Movement accords with the event; thus the meeting does not miss the opportune moment. (To respond immediately upon being moved is to grasp the essential meaning above; below is the description of the calculation.

Because the meeting does not miss the opportune moment, there must be a meeting at that which can be met. (This means there must certainly be an opportunity to meet. Because one knows there is nothing left behind, there must necessarily be...

To know is to know that which can be known (meaning there must necessarily be a knowing mind that knows the object that can be known). There must necessarily be knowing of that which can be known; therefore, the Sage’s knowing is not in vain.

There must necessarily be meeting with that which can be met; therefore, the Sage’s meeting is not in vain (meaning that since there is knowing and meeting, there must necessarily be objects that can be known and objects that can be met).

This means that knowing is not empty knowing, and realization is not empty realization. (The following is the formal objection: Since there is both knowing and realization, why do you say there is "no knowing" and "no realization"?

(This is the formal statement of the objection. Since there is both knowing and meeting, to say they do not exist—is this not erroneous? Below follows the rebuttal. As for those who forget knowing and relinquish meeting, it means that the Sage has no private attachment to knowing and meeting, yet thereby accomplishes his own true self.

(This is the rebuttal. It means that if one uses "forgetting knowing and relinquishing meeting" as a defense, then although the Sage possesses knowing and meeting, he does not boast of them as his own ability;

instead, he returns to accomplish the very reputation of knowing and meeting. The phrase "no private attachment accomplishes the private self" originates from the *Laozi*: "He puts himself last and thus is first; he regards himself as outside and thus survives.")

"Preserved. It means that when one does not prize or cherish one's own person, the person is instead preserved. This implies that the Sage merely does not boast of his cognitive realization as a private possession; therefore, people attribute their cognitive realizations to him. In reality, it is not that he lacks cognitive realization.

This may be called "not possessing one's own knowledge," but how could it be "having no knowledge"? (This is a turn to refute [the objection]. It means: as in the rescue provided above, the Sage does not boast of or rely upon cognitive realization as his own excellence;

this may be called "not possessing one's own knowledge," but how can it be said that he has no knowledge? [The following section answers by examining the characteristics of knowledge and non-knowledge. The answer says: (This answers by taking the ultimate truth [paramārtha-satya] as the basis for the possibility of extinguishing knowledge while still possessing it. First...)
Establishing the Principle: Now, the Sage’s merit surpasses that of the two polarities [Heaven and Earth]—yet he is not benevolent (the Great Benevolence is non-benevolent).

His clarity exceeds that of the sun and moon—yet he is ever more obscure. (His "merit surpasses" refers to his skillful means (*upāya*) responding to phenomena; his "clarity exceeds" refers to his ultimate wisdom (*jñāna*) realizing the Truth. Because he responds through non-action (*wuwei*), he is "not benevolent"; because he knows without deliberation, he is "ever more obscure.

How could it be said that he is like wood or stone, blinding those who harbor feelings toward him? It is simply that he is without conscious knowledge (this distinguishes him from the insentient; if one were to say he is without knowledge, he would not differ from wood or stone). This is truly because...

That which distinguishes [the Buddha] from humans is his spiritual intelligence; therefore, he cannot be sought through phenomenal characteristics. (This selects him as distinct from sentient beings. If one were to say that he possesses cognition...)
This is not the intention of ordinary people, who wish to make it appear that the Sage does not take pride in possessing knowledge; yet, the Sage has never been without knowledge.
(This restates the point of the objection: if this were considered "attainment," would it not contradict the Sage’s own mind and miss the essential meaning of the text?)

(To hold him collectively responsible is not only to fail to understand the Sage’s intent, but also to miss the meaning of the text. Why is this? (This is an exegesis that addresses the objection. The Sūtra says: "True Prajñā is pure like space;

it is without cognition, without vision, without activity, and without conditions. This means that since [Prajñā] is itself without cognition, how could one wait for a "reflexive illumination" (*pratyavekṣaṇa*) before it becomes non-cognitive?

(This citation from the Sūtra establishes that Prajñā merely lacks the cognition that grasps at delusions; it does not mean that true cognition is utterly non-existent. [The following] is a citation of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and other texts which states:

True Prajñā intends to depart from delusion; because its essence is free from even the slightest speck of dust, it is pure like space. Because it is devoid of deluded grasping, it is without knowledge and without vision. Because it is not a conditioned phenomenon, it is without action and without conditions.

Viewed through this lens, the true knowledge of Prajñā shines forth alone; it is simply that knowledge is itself non-knowing. How could one wait for the extinction of spiritual luminosity before it becomes non-knowing? If there were a nature of knowing that was empty and thus called "pure," [it would not be true Prajñā].

(This is a restatement of the opponent’s rebuttal. It means: "If one asserts that *prajñā* truly possesses cognition, yet calls it pure solely because its nature is empty... This is a counter-reproach. (It means:

"If one takes the emptiness of the nature of *prajñā* to be purity, then one cannot distinguish between delusion and wisdom. Since afflictions (*kleśa*) are also empty by nature, how could they be called *prajñā*? The three poisons and the four inversions are likewise all pure. Why then is *prajñā* alone held in such high esteem?
If you claim that *prajñā* is pure because its nature is empty, then the three poisons and the four inversions are also all empty by nature. If this were so, then [the truth would be]..."

If there is no distinction between the false and the real, why is it that only Prajñā is honored? If one praises Prajñā on account of the "truth" (*tattva*) that is known, this is a further defense [of the position].

That is to say, if one takes the purity of the truth known as the basis for praising Prajñā as being pure, [the response is: that which is known (the truth) is not Prajñā. (The truth is the object of observation; Prajñā is the observing mind.

Since the mind and its object are not identical, [the truth] is not Prajñā. Since that which is known is inherently and eternally pure, Prajñā has never been pure. (This means that if one praises Prajñā because the truth is pure, [it is incorrect].)

In its true nature (*tattva*), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is inherently and eternally pure. Now, when it is taken as an object of contemplation, the duality of subject and object has not yet been forgotten; thus, this prajñā has not yet attained purity, and so the ultimate truth, in turn, becomes a burden to the prajñā.

Furthermore, there is no cause (*hetu*) by which one could bring about purity and thereby praise the prajñā. (If the ultimate truth were to burden the prajñā, then there would likewise be no cause for purifying it so as to praise the prajñā. This is the formal explanation below.
However, when the Sūtra says that prajñā is pure, does it not mean that because the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of prajñā is truly pure, it is fundamentally free from deluded grasping?

"Knowledge. This is the knowledge that is fundamentally free from deluded grasping; it cannot be called "knowledge" by name. (This is the direct explanation of the meaning of the Sūtra. The Sūtra says, "Prajñā is pure.

Is this not because the nature of Prajñā is inherently pure and fundamentally lacks the knowledge of deluded grasping? Since there is no knowledge of deluded grasping, can it be designated by the name "true knowledge"? It is simply that there is no false knowledge, not that there is no true knowledge. Thus it is. How could it be that there is no knowledge by name and yet there is no knowing?
Knowing itself is non-knowing. (Why limit "non-knowing" to a state of absolute lack of cognition? It is truly because true knowledge is inherently devoid of false knowledge.)
Therefore, the sage uses the prajñā that is without cognition to illuminate the true dharma (tattva) that is without marks.

In this true dharma, there is no trace of the hare or the horse; in prajñā, there is no reflection that does not penetrate to the depths. Thus, they meet without deviation and accord without assertion.
It is quiescent and devoid of cognition, yet there is nothing it does not know.
This concludes the response to the question. It means that the wisdom which contemplates is without knowing, and the principle which is contemplated is without marks.
By using wisdom that is without knowing to illumine a principle that is without marks, the mind and its object are thus in suchness (*tathatā*); they form a single path, level and uniform.

Therefore, the principle transcends the traces of the three vehicles—the rabbit and the horse being metaphors for the varying depths of the three vehicles—while Prajñā illuminates everything without exception;

thus, there is no insight that does not penetrate to the ultimate. In this way, expedient wisdom responds to the various capacities of beings without error, and in every encounter it accords with reality without [clinging to] "is-ness. True wisdom, however, is quiescent and unmoving.
Being profoundly still and non-active, one thus possesses no knowledge yet knows all things. Such is the wisdom of the sage.
How could it be that not boasting of one's knowledge constitutes "no-knowledge"? Nor could it be that a total absence of knowledge constitutes "no-knowledge."

The Objection states: (This objection challenges the mutual contradiction between the two names. The questioner employs conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) to seek the reality behind the name, thereby challenging the discrepancy between the name and the reality. The following response answers by employing the two names in a way that establishes their correspondence.

Now, things have no means of communicating with one another; therefore, names are established to facilitate communication regarding things. (Things are fundamentally not names, yet they are accessed through names. Although things are not names, there must indeed be nameable things corresponding to these names.
(Names do not summon in vain; there must be a thing to correspond to them. It is like calling out "A" or "B," where someone responds. This is so.

To seek an object by means of its name, the object cannot be hidden. (This establishes the principle: according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), where there is a name, there must be an object. This raises an objection against Prajñā:

since it possesses its actual reality, to now say that it has no cognition is for the name to exist in vain while the reality is absent. Next, the objection is presented. Yet the Treatise says, "The Sage’s mind has no cognition," and also says, "There is nothing he does not know.

(This points out a mutual contradiction. The intended meaning is that "no-cognition" never fails to cognize, and "cognition" never fails to be no-cognition; this is the teaching of names and instruction.

This is what is meant by "that which is penetrated. It is the fundamental intent behind the establishment of these words. (The meaning of the critic’s objection is as follows: if one says there is no knowing, then there has never been knowing;

if one says there is knowing, then there has never been a lack of knowing. This is the purport of the establishment of the teachings. However, the debater wishes to unify [the state] with the Sage’s mind while differing from the literal meaning of the text.

Seeking the reality by following the text, I do not see this as being correct. (This is precisely a contradiction. If the Sage’s mind were one, then names should not differ. Why? If knowing were attained within the Sage’s mind, there would be...

If knowing is non-discriminating, then even the absence of knowing must accord with the Sage’s mind; yet if knowing is also non-discriminating, then if both are entirely absent, there is nothing further to discuss.

(This objection seeks to establish that the Sage’s mind must necessarily reside in one state: namely, if knowing accords with the Sage’s mind, it need not be described as "non-knowing"; conversely, if non-knowing accords with the Sage’s mind...)

[Objection: "Then one need not say that it exists. If neither existence nor non-existence accords with reality, then there is no further basis for debate. Now, to say 'knowing yet without knowing' involves two contradictory statements; how can this be a correct discourse? [Response:

This is an answer by way of conformity and fulfillment (*anuloma-siddhi-pratibhāṣa*). Since it refers to the signless nature of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), knowledge cannot be sought through names. To refute [the objection], the Sūtra says: "The meaning of *prajñā* is nameless and ineffable;

it is neither existent nor non-existent, neither real nor unreal. While being unreal, it does not lose its illumination; while illuminating, it does not lose its unreality. This, then, is the dharma that is without name.

Therefore, it is not something that can be expressed by words. (This citation of scripture establishes the principle to refute the objection. However, the objector seeks reality through names, and thus charges that existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory. Now, the meaning of the scripture is cited.)

This means that Prajñā is nameless; therefore, it cannot be sought through substantiality. It is without speech; therefore, it cannot be attained through words. Since existence and non-existence, the empty and the real—all are not [it], it is simply that its essence is empty yet does not lose its illuminating function.

Although it illuminates and responds to the myriad phenomena, it does not depart from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). This nameless Dharma is truly impossible to transmit through words. Yet, although words cannot express it, there is no way to transmit it except through words.
Therefore, the sage speaks all day long yet never speaks. Now, let me attempt to explain this for you with "mad words" (the Way is fundamentally wordless;

it is not through words that it is revealed. The sage dwells in the Way beyond words, and thus speaks all day long yet never speaks. I shall now attempt to clarify this with "mad words," which is to say, to speak of his wordlessness). As for the Sage’s mind: (This is the formal answer below;

first, it reveals that the Sage’s mind is the dual transcendence of existence and non-existence, thereby dispelling names. It is subtle and wondrous, without marks, and cannot be said to exist. (The Sage’s mind, as true wisdom, is free from marks.)
It is not comparable to conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), for it cannot be sought through names. The more one applies it with diligence, the more it cannot be regarded as non-existent;

because its provisional wisdom (upāya-prajñā) is applied so that its function never misses the mark, it cannot be regarded as non-existent—thus, sagely wisdom (ārya-jñāna) exists therein. Because its numinous awareness shines alone, it cannot be regarded as existent—thus, names and teachings are cut off therein. It merely illuminates objects through emptiness;

although its great function is brilliantly manifest, linguistic expression cannot reach it, and the path of names and words is severed. Therefore, knowing through words is not true knowing; this is intended to facilitate its penetration.

The mirror reflects by means of its emptiness; thus it is said that "knowing" is not truly having knowledge. It is merely the provisional use of the word "knowing" to explain the function of its reflective illumination. It is not that there is no knowing; it is simply that there is no [substantial] knowing.

One seeks to discern its characteristics. (This does not mean that one is utterly without knowledge; rather, it uses the word "non-" to discern the characteristic of knowing that is free from delusive grasping. Discerning the characteristics does not constitute non-existence.

(It merely lacks the characteristic of false-knowing; it is not an absolute absence of true knowing. Universal illumination does not constitute existence. (Because it illuminates objects through emptiness, it is not an existent knowing that can be grasped. Because it is not existent, there is knowing while being without knowing.
(Because the substance of true illumination is empty, although there is knowing, there is no knowing. Because it is not non-existent, there is being without knowing while knowing. (This means...)

As for "non-existence," because there is no deluded cognition, true cognition shines forth all the more. Thus, cognition is itself non-cognition, and non-cognition is itself cognition; they cannot be said to be different.

And this differs from the Sage’s mind (for it is because the Sage’s mind has truly exhausted delusion and reached the ultimate truth; its true knowledge shines alone, not falling into the extremes of existence or non-existence. How could it differ from the Sage’s mind by means of provisional words intended for negation?).

Objection: (To seek knowledge by means of causal conditions is difficult. This refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as the object of cognition (*ālambana*). Since there is an object, there must necessarily be a cognizing wisdom (*jñāna*); it is not that there is no knowledge. Now, the ultimate truth is profound and mysterious;

it cannot be fathomed except by wisdom. The capacity of noble wisdom (*ārya-jñāna*) is manifested therein. (This means that without wisdom, one cannot illuminate the ultimate truth. Therefore, a sutra says:

If one does not attain *prajñā*, one does not perceive the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Ultimate truth is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for *prajñā* (the clarity of the object and the knowing subject).

Seeking wisdom through its conditions, wisdom is indeed knowing. (This means that ultimate truth is the objective field and *prajñā* is the subjective wisdom that takes it as its object; by seeking wisdom through its conditions, wisdom is simply knowing. How could there be no knowing?

This establishes the objection based on the opposition between mind and object. The response says: (This answers by asserting that where there are no conditions, there is no knowing. The intent is that since ultimate truth is free from conditions, wisdom is likewise not "knowing. Seeking wisdom through conditions, wisdom...

"It is not knowing. (This restates the objection to refute its incorrectness, meaning: if one seeks wisdom by relying on conditions, yet the ultimate truth transcends conditions, then wisdom is likewise not "knowing.

Why is this? (This is the inquiry and explanation. The *Prabhāsa-prabhā* states: "When consciousness does not arise conditioned by form, this is called 'not seeing form. (The text says: "When consciousness is not produced through the causes and conditions of the five aggregates, this is called 'not seeing the five aggregates.

This means that when one does not give rise to discrimination based on the five aggregates, because one is detached from body and mind, one does not see the marks of body and mind; this is knowledge that transcends conditions and cannot be sought through conditions. It further states: "The five aggregates are pure..."

Because it is pure, Prajñā is pure. (Purity is another name for emptiness. Since the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are fundamentally empty, Prajñā is also empty. Being empty, it is free from conditions; it is not a cognition [that exists]. Prajñā is that which knows;

the five aggregates are that which is known. That which is known is the condition (*pratyaya*). (This establishes the relationship between the knower and the condition in order to clarify that there is no cognition apart from conditions. This means:

if one seeks to know by means of conditions, then Prajñā would be the cognition that takes those as its objects, and the five aggregates would be the objects of that cognition. Now, since it is said that the five aggregates are fundamentally empty, they are not objects of cognition. Since the object of cognition is empty, then [the subject... )

Conditions are also empty. Because they are empty, there is nothing to be known. Since one perceives that all things are empty, one knows that this very knowing is itself non-knowing; it is simply that [knowing] does not arise from conditions. Now, as for "knowing" (the mind that is able to know) and the "known" (the object):

(The objects of knowledge) exist through mutual dependence; they do not exist through mutual dependence. Because they do not exist through mutual dependence, no thing (the term "thing" here encompasses both mind and object) exists [since both mind and object are ultimately real and thus not existent].
Because they exist through mutual dependence, no thing does not exist [since mind and object stand in opposition, their relative existence is not non-existent].
Because no thing does not exist, it arises from conditions [if mind and object are not forgotten, then false conditions arise]. Because no thing exists...

Therefore, that which cannot be produced by conditions is such that when mind and object are both forgotten, the essence of illumination stands alone; it does not exist because of objects, nor is it produced by borrowing from conditions.

Because it cannot be produced by conditions, illumination upon conditions is not "knowing" (for the wisdom detached from conditions illuminates the realm of quiescent extinction, and thus there is nothing known).

Because it arises in dependence on conditions, knowing arises through the mutual causality of conditions and appearances (for when the deluded mind arises in opposition to conditions, mind and object are not yet forgotten; thus knowing arises in mutual dependence upon conditions and appearances. This is delusion and not reality). Below...

(Dual Binding and Explanation for Completion) Therefore, one knows that "false knowledge" (*mṛṣājñāna*) and "non-knowledge" (*ajñāna*) [which is true knowledge] arise from the "object of knowledge" (*jñeya*; here, the object encompasses both the real and the false). (This explains that the preceding mind and objects exist in mutual dependence.

Thus, because the deluded mind grasps at marks, there is "knowledge. Because true knowledge is free from conditions, it is "non-knowledge. This is why both knowledge and non-knowledge are all caused by the mind and its objects; there is only the matter of grasping or not grasping. Why is this? (A general inquiry into the real and the false:

Now, as for wisdom (*jñāna*), it is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) because it takes the "object of knowledge" (*jñeya*) as its cause and grasps its marks (because it possesses a counterpart, it is so named).

Deluded cognition [perceives] that the True Reality (*tattva*) is inherently without marks (*animitta*). Since there are no marks to be grasped, by what means could true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) know it? (Because the True Reality is free from marks, true wisdom is without knowing;

because it is without objects of perception, it is without knowing. *Next, the true and the deluded are distinguished individually. First, the deluded is distinguished.*) The reason it is so is explained as follows:

That which is known—the deluded object—is not truly known (because the deluded object is fundamentally empty, it is originally not an object of knowledge). The object of knowledge arises from the knowing subject (the deluded mind that is capable of knowing).

When the knowing of the delusive object arises, the knowing of the delusive mind also gives rise to that which is known—the delusive object. Thus, the delusive object and the delusive mind mutually give rise to one another.

(The deluded mind and deluded objects arise in mutual dependence. Their mutual arising constitutes the *pratyaya-dharma* (conditioned phenomena). (Mind and object depend upon one another; they arise through causes and conditions. Thus, as long as this duality is not forgotten, it is considered a *pratyaya-dharma*.

Because it is a *pratyaya-dharma*, it is not real. [Conditioned phenomena produced by conditions are provisional and not real. Because it is not real, it is not the *paramārtha-satya* (Ultimate Truth). [The opponent takes the Ultimate Truth to be the object of cognition (*ālambana*).

Now, the response is that what arises from conditions is a false phenomenon and not the Ultimate Truth. How then can it serve as an object? Therefore, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* says: (Universally proving both the real and the false: "Things exist due to causes and conditions; therefore, they are not..."

Reality (tattva). (This realized object-condition is a false phenomenon) and does not exist through causes and conditions; therefore, it is reality itself. (This realization, being free from conditions, is reality—hereafter, reality is revealed.

Now, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is called "reality. Being reality, it is not a condition. (Being reality, it does not arise by borrowing conditions. Reality is not a condition. (Since the ultimate truth is not a condition) there is no entity that arises from conditions.

(Previously, the opponent took the ultimate truth as a condition, and thus regarded Prajñā as having cognition. Now, the Master of the Treatise answers that the ultimate truth is free from conditions. How could the ultimate truth, which is free from conditions, give rise to Prajñā?)

"You know that [things] arise from conditions; you should rather say they arise from non-conditions. This means that there is not a single dharma that arises from non-conditions. The intent is to rebuke the objector for failing to comprehend the True Dharma (satyadharma) and for falsely speculating on something apart from conditions. Therefore, the Sūtra says:

One does not perceive any phenomenon that exists without conditions (this is not so). [All things] arise through conditions. (This establishes the aforementioned principle: if conditions cannot produce phenomena, then ultimate truth, being devoid of conditions, would necessarily never give rise to cognition.
Therefore, when true wisdom contemplates ultimate truth, it never grasps that which is known (meaning that when true wisdom illuminates ultimate truth, it never takes it as an object of knowledge).

If wisdom does not grasp that which is known, by what means could this wisdom know? (Since true wisdom does not grasp an object of knowledge, by what means could this wisdom possibly know? Yet, wisdom is not...

"Non-knowing. (This negates an error. It means that true wisdom merely does not apprehend the objects of knowledge; it is not that the substance of knowing is utterly non-existent. This is because "knowing" consists in solitary illumination, which is independent of anything else.

However, the True Truth is not an object of knowledge (it means that the True Truth is signless and is not an object within the sphere of knowledge). Therefore, true wisdom is also not "knowing" (because the True Truth is not an object of knowledge, true wisdom is likewise not "knowing").
These two phrases conclude the subtle mystery of the non-knowing of Prajñā. (Below follows the reprimand. Yet you wish to seek wisdom through conditions; therefore, by means of wisdom...
[Objection: "If wisdom (*jñāna*) is non-conceptual while cognition (*jñā*) is conceptual, then by taking cognition for wisdom, truth and delusion would not be distinguished.

Why then do you raise this objection? [Response: "Cognition seeks [its object] through conditions, yet those conditions are themselves not conditions. Seeking it through what, then, could one know it? This means that both object and wisdom are simultaneously forgotten, and subject and object are equally extinguished.
The profound purport of Prajñā reaches its ultimate subtlety here."

The Objection states: (The previous argument spoke of "non-apprehending cognition"; now, it is argued that whether one has cognition or lacks it, non-apprehension is in both cases untenable. This constitutes a double-pronged objection. The Treatise says, "Non-apprehension" (this cites the treatise to present the objection).

Is it because of a lack of cognition that there is no apprehension? Or is it that one first possesses cognition and then refrains from apprehending? (This establishes the basis for the following objection.

If it is because of a lack of cognition that there is no apprehension, then the Sage would be as oblivious as one wandering at night, unable to distinguish between black and white, would he not? (This would mean he is in a state of blinding ignorance. If, however, he does possess cognition...

"Then one does not grasp. To have knowledge is different from not grasping. (This means that if there is knowledge, there must be an object to be grasped; since knowledge already exists, it is difficult to say one does not grasp.

[The preceding section refuted the position by showing the duality of mind and object; the following answers by showing the unity of mind and object. The answer says: (One answers by asserting that neither existence nor non-existence constitutes non-grasping.

It is not because of a lack of knowledge that one does not grasp, nor is it because of having knowledge that one subsequently does not grasp. (Neither existence nor non-existence constitutes non-grasping. Knowledge itself is non-grasping; therefore, one is able to not grasp."
"Knowing this clarifies both [aspects]. That is to say, by knowing the locus, one does not grasp it in the present; therefore, one is able to know without grasping. Objection:
"Because one has heard that the preceding mind and its objects are both non-existent, one argues that since neither the mind nor its objects are grasped, both must be annihilated. The Treatise says:

"As for 'not grasping,' it is truly because the Sage’s mind does not objectify things (i.e., does not cling to them), and thus there is no deluded grasping. (The first part establishes the principle; the second part presents the objection. If there is no grasping, then there is no "is-ness."

(“Is” [shi] is a designation for the non-erroneous realization of things; it is the mind capable of such knowledge. Without “is,” there is no “correspondence” [dang]. (Correspondence means responding to things without error; it is the primary substance without deviation. It refers to the realm that is known.

Who corresponds to the Sage’s mind? (This means: if there were no realm to be known, who could correspond to the Sage’s mind? If there were no realm to which the mind could correspond, would this not be nihilism? Yet you say, “The Sage’s mind knows nothing it does not know.

(If there were no realm to which the Sage’s mind could correspond, then it would be utterly devoid of anything known. To then say it “knows nothing it does not know”—is this not erroneous? He replied: (I answer with the correspondence of the Perfect Unity.)
Indeed. (This is a concessive expression. There is neither "is" nor "is not. (This restates the meaning of the objection. Now, if there is no "is not," then there is nothing that is not [as it is].

(To say "is" means to accord with the realm of the mind. If a single realm accords with the mind, one becomes stuck and lacks penetration. If there is no mind with which to accord, then the realm is tranquil and the mind is empty. The true mind functions as universal cognition; therefore, there is nothing that is not as it is.

If there is no "is," then there is nothing that is not [so]. (This means that when there is no grasping mind, the mind is empty and the realm is tranquil. All phenomena are thus truly real; therefore, there is nothing that is not so. Because there is nothing that is not so, it is "is."

Yet there is no such thing [as "is"]. (When one realizes that objects are but mind, then both mind and object are forgotten; right and wrong are equally extinguished. Thus, even "is" is not "is. There is nothing that is not appropriate, yet it is appropriate without being appropriate.

(Because the realm is but mind, there is no longer any object outside the mind that can serve as a condition for the mind. Thus, although it illumines objects, all phenomena are empty. Therefore, it is appropriate without being appropriate.

Hence the Sūtra says: "To see all dharmas exhaustively, yet to see nothing. (Since all dharmas are but mind, there is not a single dharma that can be grasped by the emotions. Therefore, one sees all dharmas exhaustively, yet sees nothing.)

The objection states: (Having heard that both mind and objects are extinguished, one consequently suspects that one abandons existence to enter non-existence; thus, an objection is raised. It is not that the Sage’s mind is incapable of this [realization];

rather, it is truly because there is no "is" by which to affirm it. (This describes how the Sage’s mind abandons existence to grasp the essential meaning. Although there is no "is" by which to affirm it, (this is granted as established) one must therefore affirm it within non-being.

(This is taken as entering into non-existence. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Because the True Truth is without marks, Prajñā is without cognition. (This citation proves non-cognition; this describes the intent of what has been grasped.)
Truly, in Prajñā there is no cognition characterized by existence. (This explains the correct meaning of the sūtra; the following uses a mistaken interpretation to raise an objection.

If one takes non-characteristic as being non-characteristic, what harm does this do to the True Truth? (The intent is: if having characteristics were to harm Prajñā, then now, if one takes non-characteristic as being non-characteristic, what harm does that do to Prajñā?

This fails to realize that the true cognition of Prajñā shines forth alone, and thus takes absolute nothingness to be Prajñā. He replies: (It is difficult to enter non-existence by abandoning existence; the reply is that both [existence and non-existence] are lost, which is non-characteristic. The Sage...

A person does not lack the signless (*animitta*). (The opponent recognizes the signless; the respondent answers that even the signless is non-existent. This is a comprehensive response to the intent of the question. Why? (This interrogates and explains why even the signless is not [existent].

If one takes the signless to be the signless, (if one clings to the signless, then the mind has a place of abiding; the Sage’s mind is not thus. The signless then becomes a sign. (If one grasps and clings to the signless, then the signless itself becomes a sign.
Yongjia said: "Abandoning existence to cling to emptiness is likewise a sickness. To abandon existence and go toward non-existence is like fleeing from a mountain peak only to...

Entering a ravine, both are inevitably subject to calamity (just as it is like avoiding drowning only to throw oneself into fire). This refers to the annihilationism of the non-Buddhists; how could the Sage’s mind be such? (The following explains that the Sage’s mind abides nowhere.

Therefore, the Perfected Person dwells amidst existence yet does not exist; resides in non-existence yet does not not exist. (Though they traverse existence and non-existence, they do not abide in existence or non-existence—this is what is meant by "not abiding in the two extremes.

Although they do not grasp at existence or non-existence, they likewise do not abandon existence or non-existence. (Not abiding in existence or non-existence, they do not even settle in the Middle Way.)

Therefore, he harmonizes his light with worldly toil (Laozi says: "harmonize his light and be one with the dust"). He circulates through the five realms of existence (this is the capacity for conditioned action).

He proceeds in stillness (unmoving from the fundamental limit, yet manifesting in all things). He arrives in a state of quietude (where the myriad transformations do not shift, as the mind is merged with the transcendent realm).
He is tranquil and non-active, yet there is nothing he does not do (the Sage takes non-abiding as his mind; how could he be modeled by the categories of existence or non-existence?).

The Objection states: (This objection arises from the difficulty of reconciling provisional wisdom with arising and ceasing; it is raised because one has not yet realized that movement and stillness are of one suchness.

Although the Sage’s mind is without cognition, the Way by which it responds to and accords with circumstances does not err. (This summarizes the essential point. Therefore, that which is capable of being responded to is responded to; that which cannot be responded to is left as it is.

(This [objection] suspects that the Sage’s mind discriminates between what is acceptable and what is not, and thus concludes that there is arising and ceasing. If this is so, then the Sage’s mind must at times arise and at times cease. Is this not the case?

"Is this not so? (This objection is raised because one has not yet realized that birth is fundamentally non-arising. The answer says: (The answer is that the Sage’s mind is fundamentally without arising or ceasing.

As for 'arising and ceasing,' these belong to the mind of arising and ceasing (which is the mind of ordinary beings). How could a Sage be like this? The Sage is without mind; how then could arising and ceasing arise? (Thus, true reality manifests as non-arising. Yet, it is not that there is no mind."

(Unlike wood or stone, which are insentient,) it is simply that there is no mind that is not mind. (It is simply that the absence of a mind of arising and ceasing constitutes "mind. Furthermore, it is not that there is no response.

(Unlike being solitary and unattended,) it is simply that there is no responding that is not a response. (It is simply to respond according to conditions as they arise; fundamentally, there is no mind of welcoming or sending off.

Therefore, the Way by which the Sage responds to the convergence of circumstances is as trustworthy as the substance of the four seasons. (Substance means reality. Because the Sage’s mind has no causal conditions for responding to things, yet he penetrates them as soon as he is moved, like an echo in a valley or the moon in water, he is thus trustworthy.)
The reality of the four seasons should not miss its proper time; it takes emptiness (śūnyatā) and quiescent extinction (nirvāṇa) as its essence.

Thus, it cannot be produced and cannot be extinguished (for, through the true knowledge of quiescent extinction, it manifests in accordance with conditions; therefore, fundamentally there is no arising or ceasing).
Objection: (Having heard that there is neither arising nor ceasing, yet not yet having realized that both delusion and wisdom are empty, I therefore offer this objection:

If the non-existence of sagely wisdom and the non-existence of deluded wisdom (as previously stated—that sagely wisdom lacks the cognition of grasping at delusion, and thus there is no cognition of grasping at delusion)—are both devoid of arising and ceasing, how can they be distinguished? (This means: fundamental ultimate wisdom has a solitary, numinous discernment;

being originally without cognition, it is called the "non-existence of sagely wisdom. Subsequently attained provisional wisdom illuminates and shatters ignorance; since delusive confusion is fundamentally empty, there is no cognition of grasping at delusion. Since both are non-existent, if one does not understand the meaning of "non-existence," how can one differentiate between them? Thus, this objection is raised. Response:

It is said: (First, the delusion of wisdom and the non-wisdom of the Sage are distinguished together to demonstrate the varying depths of the meaning of emptiness. That which is the "non-existence" of Sage-wisdom is "non-knowing. (True knowledge shines alone; since both mind and object are forgotten, it is called "non-knowing. That which is the "non-existence" of deluded wisdom is "knowing that there is nothing.

(Expedient wisdom illuminates and shatters the false knowing of grasping at delusions, realizing their original non-existence; thus, it is called "knowing that there is nothing. Although their non-existence is the same, the reasons for this non-existence differ.

(Sage-knowledge is naturally non-knowing and does not rely on effort or achievement; the non-wisdom of delusion is attained through cultivation. Thus, while the state of non-existence is the same, the underlying principles are different. Why is this so?

(Explaining the Difference) Now, the Sage’s mind is empty and still; there is no cognition that can be negated, which may be called "non-cognition," yet this does not mean that cognition is non-existent.

(The Sage’s true mind is uniquely luminous, tranquil and unmoving, utterly devoid of delusive phenomena; therefore, there is no cognition to be negated, and it may simply be called "non-cognition. One cannot say that cognition is non-existent.

Delusion and wisdom possess cognition, so there is cognition that can be negated, which may be called "the non-existence of cognition," but this is not what is meant by "non-cognition. (Subsequently, one illuminates delusion and realizes that the false is fundamentally empty; one may only say that the false was originally non-existent, but...)
One may speak of "non-cognition," yet this non-cognition is precisely the emptiness of *prajñā*. (*Prajñā* is fundamentally beyond all delusions; therefore, it cannot be said that it knows emptiness.

This "knowing emptiness" is precisely the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). (To "know emptiness" means to know that the ultimate truth is devoid of deluded cognition. Thus, between *prajñā* and the ultimate truth—(from here below, the mind and its objects are clarified in unison, meeting the identity and difference of quiescence and function;

first, identity and difference are explained together)—if one speaks of function, they are identical yet different (being quiescent yet illuminating); if one speaks of quiescence, they are different yet... [identical].
It is identical. (That is, it is illumination while being quiescent. Because it is identical, there is no mind regarding self and other. (This refers to the mind and its objects;

when identical, both mind and object are simultaneously extinguished. Because it is different, the function of illumination is not lost. (Object and wisdom are clearly distinct. Therefore, those who discern identity find identity within difference (identifying that which is not identical).

Those who discern difference find difference within identity (differentiating that which is not different). (In this, both mind and object coexist, and illumination and function are simultaneous. Thus, it cannot be differentiated, nor can it be...

They are identical. (Because both are neither-dual-nor-extinguished, they cannot be definitively named as either identical or different. Why is this? (To subtly distinguish between quiescence and function: Internally, there is the clarity of solitary discernment; (standing alone as the illuminating essence, it is quiescence.
Externally, there is the reality of the myriad dharmas; (all dharmas are true, which is function. Although the myriad dharmas are real, they cannot be attained without illumination.

(Although the myriad dharmas are real, their reality cannot be attained without the illumination of wisdom. Internally (the mind) and externally (the objects) cooperate to accomplish the function of illumination.

(When wisdom attains the objects, the function of illumination is fully manifested; when the objects attain wisdom, the true permanence is uniquely revealed. Thus it is said that internally and externally they cooperate to accomplish this function. This is the "function" which even sages cannot share.

(Without objects there would be no way to manifest wisdom; therefore, they cannot be shared. Although internally there is illumination, there is no cognition (not a cognition of dualistic opposition). Although externally there is reality, there are no marks (all dharmas...).

The true mark (*dharmatā*) cannot be sought through marks; therefore, it is said to be "markless. Internally and externally, all is tranquil. (Internally, wisdom is without cognition; externally, objects are without marks. Since mind and object are both extinguished, it is called "tranquility. Mark and [the absence of] mark are both non-existent.

(Because the mind is empty, the object is tranquil; because the object is tranquil, the mind is empty. Thus, mind and object are together leveled as one path. This is that which even the sages cannot differentiate.

It is quiescence. (In quiescence, both mind and object vanish; therefore, they cannot be differentiated. Thus, when the Sūtra says that "all dharmas are not different," does it mean that one must first lengthen the legs of a duck or shorten those of a crane, or level a mountain peak and fill a valley, before they become non-different?

(This citation proves that they are fundamentally non-different. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "All dharmas are without marks; they are neither of one mark nor of different marks. Regarding the phrase "How could it be said...": this citation explains why they are not different. The *Zhuangzi* says:

"Though the duck's legs are short, to lengthen them causes distress; though the crane's legs are long, to cut them off causes grief. This means that what Heaven has made long or short need not be adjusted to equality. A mountain peak is high and a valley is low by nature—) ...fundamentally [they are so].)

This arises from meditative concentration (*samādhi*). It does not require leveling the heights of mountains to fill the depths of ravines; rather, its intent is to lead one to realize that all phenomena are, in their very essence, true and eternal, fundamentally without differentiation. As it is said: "These dharmas abide in their own dharma-position; the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding," requiring no deliberate effort or fabrication.

Thereafter, they are equalized. This means that when the wisdom of non-duality illuminates the realm of the one true reality, every phenomenon is truly eternal and fundamentally not different. This is spontaneous non-differentiation; it is not a state of non-differentiation achieved through deliberate arrangement.

Because it is not different from difference, although there is difference, there is no difference. (Because one does not allow the mind to differ according to the differences in objects, the objects follow the mind as one;

thus, though different, they are identical, which is why it is said: "although different, they are not different. Therefore, a sutra says: "How marvelous, World-Honored One! Within the dharma of non-difference, you have spoken of all dharmas."

"Distinct. (This means that based upon the single true dharma-realm, immeasurable and differentiated dharma-gates are expounded; hence it is said: "There are no distinct dharmas, yet distinct dharmas are taught. It further says: "Prajñā and all dharmas..."

They are neither of a single characteristic nor of different characteristics. This is credible [as evidenced by various citations of their being neither one nor different]. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "World-Honored One, how can you speak of the differentiation of all phenomena within the realm of non-differentiation?

It further says: "All phenomena are without characteristics; they are not of a single characteristic, nor are they of different characteristics. Thus we know that regarding all phenomena as either identical or distinct is the false view of the non-Buddhists. When observed through Prajñā, they are neither one nor different. The ultimate principle of the *bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā* (the Prajñā of true reality) reaches its zenith here.

The Objection states: (Because one hears of both quiescence and function, one consequently suspects there are two; thus, this objection is established. The Treatise says: "To speak of function is to differ;

to speak of quiescence is to be the same. This is not yet clear: within Prajñā, is there a distinction between function and quiescence? (Failing to realize that movement and stillness share a single source, one suspects that quiescence and function are two distinct things.

The Response states: (Answering by showing that quiescence and function are of one accord. Function is itself quiescence; quiescence is itself function. Function and quiescence are one in essence; they emerge together yet bear different names. (The phrase "emerging together yet bearing different names" is a quotation from...)

Laozi said: "Being and non-being emerge together from the same mystery. This means that quiescence and function are fundamentally rooted in the One Mind; it is merely a matter of speaking in terms of movement and stillness.

There is no such thing as a quiescence devoid of function, for the primary focus is on function (meaning that the essence of quiescence must necessarily possess the function of illumination, just like the light of a bright mirror; there has never been a mirror of radiant clarity that lacked the capacity to reflect). Therefore, the more profound the wisdom, the more subtle it becomes.

The illumination becomes ever more brilliant; (this means that when true wisdom illuminates principle, the objects of knowledge are extinguished, and thus it becomes increasingly profound. Because true clarity further unfolds, the illumination becomes ever more brilliant. This refers to the function of quiescence. The spirit becomes ever more still.

"One should transcend movement. (Because true wisdom is utterly quiescent, expedient function is boundless. This statement means that function does not depart from essence; hence it says "one should transcend movement. How could this be said to be a distinction between clarity and obscurity, or movement and stillness?

(This concludes the non-duality of quiescence and function. Thus, the *Sūtra of Complete Perfection* says: "Without acting, one acts beyond measure. (This proves that expedient wisdom is the very expedient of reality. The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* says: "Without mind and without consciousness, there is nothing that is not aware and knowing.
(This proves the wisdom that is free from delusion, manifesting the function of that which is inherently quiescent. This, then, is the ultimate penetration of the spirit.

(Wisdom and skillful means respond to things) through the wisdom of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*). (True wisdom illuminates principle) and represents the ultimate discourse beyond the realm of forms. (The commentary cites two sutras to clarify both quiescence and function;
this is indeed the ultimate discourse beyond the realm of forms. By examining these explicit texts, the Sage’s mind can be known. (Viewed through this lens, all doubts will melt away like ice.)
*The Treatise on the Non-Cognition of Prajñā* (End).

Written by the Śramaṇa Hanshan Shi Deqing of Mount Kuang, Ming Dynasty.
Attached is a letter from Liu Yimin, including Yimin’s salutation: "Obeisance."
According to the new commentary: His name was Chengzhi, his courtesy name was Zhongsu, and his alternative style was Yimin (the Recluse), signifying a person who has withdrawn from the world.

He was a native of Pengcheng and a descendant of Liu Dao of Chu Yuanyou during the Han dynasty. While he was proficient in the various schools of thought externally, he internally investigated Buddhist principles.
He once served as the Magistrate of Chaisang; encountering the initial emergence of Huan Xuan’s usurpation and rebellion, he sighed, saying: "The Jin house lacks the foundation of a bedrock..."

Indeed, the common people were in as much peril as a stack of eggs; consequently, Huiyuan and other eminent figures of the era—such as the Confucian scholars Huici, Zongbing, and Zhou Xuzhi—served Master Yuan under Mount Lu, where they were known as the "Eighteen Worthies.

They diligently formed the Lotus Society, disregarding summons to official office. When the Grand Marshal Liu Yu perceived their wild aspirations and profound detachment from the world, he [honored them] for their noble aloofness.
They exchanged formal greetings. At that time, Master Daosheng entered the Guanzhong region to study under Master Kumārajīva, and he became inseparable from the Master in debate.
When Master Daosheng returned south, he presented his previous treatise to the community at Mount Lu. Huiyuan, the "Left-home Man," read it and marveled in admiration.
He presented it to Master Huiyuan. The Master sighed in admiration, saying, "This is truly unprecedented! Although this inquiry was sent by Huiran, it also reflects the profound intent of Huiyuan.

Recently, I have heard of his refined character (‘wei’ meaning flavor; ‘hui’ being a tone for a name); he harbors deep thoughts and gazes afar with longing. Before the year grows cold and harsh, [may you] maintain your health."

How is it? Our voices are stifled by distance and our hearts grow heavy with pent-up longing. This disciple has long suffered from chronic ailments in the wilds (the mountains and fields), constantly plagued by infirmities.
Only through the northern journey of the practitioner Huiming have I been able to briefly communicate my feelings.
Before setting forth the questions on the profound meaning of the teachings, I first express my greetings and my sentiments of deep admiration.

I have recently heard of your illustrious reputation, like one who, parched with hunger and thirst, finally finds food and drink; thus I say "I have eaten" (of your fame). I harbor a longing desire to see you, yet I am unable to do so, and can only gaze afar with yearning anticipation.
As the year draws to a close, I wonder how your physical well-being fares. Lacking a messenger-bird to carry this message, I remain constrained.

Thus, our voices have been obstructed by distance and failed to reach one another, while thoughts of accumulated longing have increased daily. Regretfully lying ill in the marshes, I have been unable to visit you from afar;
my feelings have not yet reached you. Recently, because Huiming traveled north, I was finally able to convey a portion of my sentiments.
This letter describes how my heart’s longings for you have remained thus even in your absence.
The ancients did not allow physical distance to cause their thoughts to grow thin; once they attained spiritual resonance, they felt intimacy.

Thus, although the rivers and mountains were vast and remote and we did not meet in person during our prime, as for my yearning for your refined character and my reflecting upon your spirit through your traces, my diligent longing was truly profound.
Being far away with no means of contact, I gaze at the clouds and sigh forever. I wish you well according to the seasons and hope that, through your travels, we may frequently [correspond].
There is a preface that conveys a sense of longing and admiration. The ancients did not allow physical distance to cause their thoughts to grow cold;
if their hearts were in accord and mutual understanding reached, they remained close despite the distance. Therefore, although mountains and rivers may be vast and remote, in the past—

Though we have not met for years, as I look up to you with longing and cherish the fragrance of your Way and the flavor of your Dharma, the mirror of my mind reflects your image and traces without ever straying from the space of a single inch.
Thus, the diligence of my waiting and gazing grows deeper by the day; such is the intensity of this yearning admiration.

My private thoughts remain deeply nostalgic and I have not forgotten you; yet, having no means to see you even once, I gaze upon the mists and clouds of Mount Qinling, which only serves to increase my sighs of longing.
My feelings of affection and reverence persist at all times without fading. I hope that, taking advantage of the convenience of passing travelers, you will send me frequent news.
I humbly pray that the great assembly may enjoy peace and harmony, and that the foreign Dharma Master may be in good health.
This is a prayer for their well-being. It is customary for the foreign Dharma Master to be in good health and receive blessings at all times;
however, because the Master of the Treatise was present at the translation hall, he inquired after the assembly and extended his greetings to his own teacher.

The Master possesses the vessel for awakening and has encountered these profound responses; I imagine that the merit of his investigation and study is sufficient to exhaust more than half of my own thoughts.
Thus, whenever I reflect upon our long separation, how deep is my resentment and shame!

This praises the good fortune of the Master of the Treatise (Sengzhao) in his encounter [with Kumārajīva]. It expresses his own sense of humility. Regarding the "vessel for awakening" (*wufa zhi qi*):
this refers to the Master having previously encountered a Brahmin teacher who brought the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Dhyānapāramitā-sūtra* to the Qin.

This mountain monk, Qingchang, is ever more diligent in his observance of the precepts. Beyond his seclusion in meditation, he devotes himself solely to study and exposition.

There are masters such as these; thus the body has something upon which to rely and the mind has something with which to find solace, thereby fulfilling one's aspirations.
To look up to the Way and depart from this world is a joy that grows ever more profound over time—this, moreover, is the great cause for celebration and fortune for Master Liu.

Section Two: Examining the Essence.

This is titled "Raising Objections," which constitutes the first part of the refutation. Because it was previously stated that the essence of *nirvāṇa* is neither existent nor non-existent, it is now refuted:
